en: The *Pañcasāyaka*, composed by Jyotīrīśvara, who bears the title *Kaviśekharatila*,
[ends with] the first arrow (*sāyaka*).
Invocation:

Victorious is the god of love, the dolphin-bannered one, the sole cause of infatuation; he is an ocean of the fragrance of passion, the intimate companion of amorous play with beautiful women, the delighter of the world, whose joy is served by all, and who is attended by many worshippers among those filled with desire. (JPanc 1.1)
The author’s presentation of his own identity:

There is on earth a virtuous man, Śrī Jyotirīśa, who is the sole initiating preceptor in the joy of removing the desires of supplicants day after day; who is devoted to the worship of Śrīkaṇṭha; who is a treasury of the sixty-four arts; who is a wish-fulfilling gem of skill in composing works on music, sacred tradition, and true principles; and whose feet are marked by the title "Crown of Poets. (JPanc_1.2)
Having examined the treatise on love composed by Īśvara, the doctrine of Vātsyāyana, the work of Goṇīputra and Mūladeva, the nectar-like words of Bābhravya,

and the teachings on the science of love spoken by the illustrious Nandīśvara and Rantideva, as well as the *Vidyāgama* of Kṣemendra, he thus composed this "Five-Arrowed One" (*Pañcasāyaka*), which bestows joy upon lovers.

The characteristics of the hero (nāyaka): He is well-behaved, compassionate, resolute, generous, pure in intention, desirable, a treasury of the arts of love, eloquent, esteemed by women, handsome, wealthy, skilled in policy, patient, curious, brave, of noble birth, young, and endowed with training in music; in brief, such is the hero described here. (JPanc 1.4)

The characteristics of the *pīṭhamarda*: He should always be one who is well-trained in conduct, discipline, and policy; sincere in the triple arts [of song, dance, and instrumental music]; unartificial in the application of treatises, curiosity, crafts, and drama; skilled in various arts; capable in the formulation of all jests through reasoning and refutation; knowing the internal states and gestures of others; clever, knowledgeable in counsel, firm in friendship, and eloquent. (JPanc 1.5)
The characteristics of the *padminī*:
She whose face is like the full moon, with tremulous eyes, full breasts, and soft limbs; who is clever, fragrant as a blooming lotus, and possesses a dark or fair complexion;
who delights in little food, is skilled in amorous play, has a voice like a swan, is proud yet modest, and is devoted to the worship of elders and gods—she is the heroine known as the *padminī*.
The characteristics of the Citriṇī:
She is dark-complexioned, lotus-faced, with eyes like those of a deer, slender-waisted, affectionate, skilled in the arts of music, and possessed of beautiful, high breasts.

Devoted to the practice of spells, she walks with the gait of an elephant and possesses a voice like the cry of a rutting peacock; she should be known as the Citriṇī, the beloved of the crest-jewels of poets, possessing a variegated voice.
The characteristics of the Śaṅkhinī:

She has slender limbs, eyes shaped like a curved hut, and small yet full breasts; she is prone to fits of passion, generally possesses long hair, and is by nature treacherous, making her difficult to enjoy in sexual union.

Tawny-eyed, with a restless gait and a gurgling voice, she delights in red garments and takes pleasure in scratching various parts of the body with her nails; such a woman is considered a Śaṅkhinī. (JPanc 1.8)

The characteristics of the *hastinī* (elephant-woman): She has a somewhat stout and small body, a very gentle gait, is cruel, and has a bent neck. Her hair is slightly reddish-brown, her breasts are large, and her face is devoid of modesty. She has lips like the *bimba* fruit, a great appetite for food, and is difficult to satisfy in sexual union. A fair-complexioned woman whose flow of passion smells like the ichor (*dāna*) of an elephant is considered a *hastinī*.
The postures that bring pleasure during sexual union for the *padminī* and other types of women are known to be fourteen, five, three, two, and fifteen lunar days respectively.
During sexual union, the *nalinī* woman finds delight on the fifth, sixth, and seventh lunar days; the *citriṇī* is pleased on the third, sixth, eighth, and twelfth lunar days;

and the *śaṅkhinī* rejoices on the eleventh, seventh, ninth, and thirteenth lunar days. For the pleasure of a woman of the *kariṇī* class, all the remaining lunar days are suitable for the festival of love.
Thus ends the section on the classification of *jāti*.
Now follows the description of the *candrakalā* (phases of the moon):
[The sequence] is declared for the thumb, the foot, the seat of the hips, the two knees, the two shanks, the navel, the chest, the two armpits, the throat, the cheek, and the lower lip.
In the eyes, the pair of ears, the surface of the forehead, and the crown of the head of those with beautiful brows, the lunar digit is said to move up and down during the two fortnights.

In the parting of the hair, the eyes, the lips, the throat, the slope of the armpits, the nipples, the navel, the slope of the hips, the abode of the mind, the slopes of the shanks, the two thighs, the ankles, the soles of the feet, the surface of the toes, and the big toes—there dwells that digit of the moon which brings delight to women, waxing and waning in accordance with these locations. (JPanc_1.12)
The procedure for kindling the digit of the moon [the female organ]:
pulling at the locks of hair on the head, kissing the eyes, pressing the cheeks with the teeth, and gently striking the heart with the fist and the navel;
nails should be applied to the armpits, throat, cheeks, breasts, and hips; one should scratch the parting of the hair with the nails and then grasp the two breasts firmly. (JPanc 1.13)
In the temple of the mind-born god, lovers should incessantly perform the playful movements of an elephant, joining their knees, big toes, feet, thighs, and ankles with one another.
Thus has been described the kindling of the digit of the moon through the union of specific body parts; however, the entire detailed elaboration is not stated here for fear of prolixity.
The *Padminī-candrakalā-pradīpana*:

Having first embraced her firmly, one should scratch the surface of her shanks with fingernails, and then, applying fine nail-marks upon the expanse of her hips, her sides, her back, and her belly—causing horripilation to arise through the sound of her gasping sighs—those who know the *candrakalā* technique should thus bring the *padminī* woman under their complete control on the first day. (JPanc_1.15)
Having kissed the sprout-like lower lip, and having made nail-marks upon the breasts, the face, the forehead, the sides, the crown of the head,

and the surface of the hips and thighs, they should, on the following day, continue to serve the gazelle-eyed woman— whose passion has fully awakened— with their nails, even as she endures them upon her pair of lotus-feet.

Embracing him most tightly and pressing his breasts, and having sipped his lip, those women skilled in the external arts of love would, on the fourth lunar day, carelessly bestow nail-marks upon the thighs of the fair-limbed one— especially at the base of her vine-like arms— and nail-marks resembling the feet of a peacock, mostly adorned with crescent moons.
Having kissed her pouty lips and drawn back her mass of hair with his right hand, he should passionately press her pair of nipples and kiss his beloved;

then, having touched the surface of her hips with his nails in a playful manner until they bristle with thrills, he should again lead her to a state of melting—Vātsyāyana says this regarding the fifth stage.
The method for awakening Citriṇī’s crescent-moon [of passion]:

the intoxicated lover, having kissed her forehead, scratches with his fingernails the surface of her breasts, the region of her hips, back, arms, feet, ears, loins, thighs, and the pair of her shanks.
On the tenth lunar day, the lover, embracing his own beloved with both hands and awakening the god of love, should make her his own Citriṇī by means of the digit of the moon.
Having firmly embraced the stalk of the neck with the noose of her vine-like arms, and repeatedly drinking the nectar from the lotus-faces of the lotus-eyed women,
let the nails— skilled in the art of the crescent moon on the sixth lunar day and expert in the maneuvers of the fingernails upon the navel, throat, and rounded hips— be applied everywhere.

Embracing her neck firmly and repeatedly scratching her navel with his nails, pressing the slope of her breasts with his teeth and lips, he should strike her throat slightly; thus, by performing the sport of an elephant's trunk in the temple of passion, he should bring the young woman under his own control on the day of the goddess Caṇḍī, when she is full of wonder. (JPanc 1.21)

On the lunar day of the Sun, the hero should forcibly embrace her, kissing her cheeks, eyes, hips, and ears; being skilled in applying his nails, he should mercilessly scratch her at those very spots, bite her sprout-like lower lip, and gradually pull her hair until he brings her under his control as she utters piteous *sīt* sounds. (Jānakīpariṇaya 1.22)
The procedure for the illumination of the *candrakalā* of the *śaṅkhinī*:

Having scratched her armpits with fingernails that have risen [with excitement] and having embraced her repeatedly and firmly with both arms, one who knows the moon should press her intensely on the lunar day of Viṣṇu;
then, kissing her cheeks, throat, and neck while massaging her two breasts, one should quickly cause the *śaṅkhinī* to melt by means of nail-marks on the lunar day of Kandarpa.
With his lips bitten and scratching his cheeks, eyes, and ears with his nails, he gazed upon the passionate woman on that lunar day of the sun, whose neck was hidden by a thick garland of joy.
Having inflicted wounds with his claws upon the navel, feet, neck, breasts, and chest, and having scratched them on the day of Bhūtanātha, the wise man shall render her utterly distraught.
The method for awakening the elephant-maiden (hastinī) like the crescent moon:

Embracing her neck with his vine-like arms, drinking from her lotus-face, and stroking with trembling nails the region of her armpits, breasts, and the slope of her belly; then repeatedly touching the temple of love while making the mountain-born maiden his guest, he should, upon the lunar day of the planet (Graha-tithi), perform the "Swift" (drutā) embrace upon biting her sprout-like lower lip. JPanc_1.26.
On the lunar day of the full moon, which is the very day of its waning, a passionate woman was brought under control by means of addresses using the name "Crescent of the Moon.
Nandīśvara says that this was done with nails and teeth upon the peaks of her breasts—the abode of desire—with bites on her lips, and with various embraces and kisses. (JPanc 1.27)
The determination of the time for sexual union for the *padminī* and other types is as follows:

the fourth watch of the night is declared the time for the *nalinī*; for her, the pleasure of love reaches its peak when the first watch has passed. For the *śaṅkhinī*, the third watch of the night is proclaimed by the best of poets as the time for lovemaking; the *mātaṅgī*, however, attains the highest state of passion at both midnight and midday. (JPanc 1.28)
A lotus-pond does not provide pleasure to a man at night through amorous dalliance; therefore, nothing at all should be pursued with her.
Even if a youth were to approach his beloved during the day, she would forcibly bloom like a lotus-pond due to the contact with the sun.
The description of the female temperament:

She whose waist is marked by three folds, who has a neck like a conch shell, who is clever, whose body is fragrant as a lotus, and who is as beautiful as the interior of a *ketakī* flower; she who is purified by pure conduct, endowed with virtue and contentment, and possesses a voice as sweet as a lovely cuckoo—such a woman is of divine temperament (*devasattva*). (JPanc 1.30)
With a gaze that is frequently flickering, skilled in dance, song, and the like, possessing a sweet and abundant fragrance, and devoted to flower garlands;
she who is the object of affection during play in the cool and fragrant months, and whose form is beautiful—she indeed is one of Gandharva nature.
Bearing the weight of her heavy breasts, fair-bodied, with limbs bent low, possessing the eyes of a young deer, irascible and devoid of shame,
speaking various sweet words, and fond of fish and meat— this woman is declared by sages to be of priceless value and of Yakṣa nature.

Those known as *preta* beings are skilled at roaming the mountains, heroes who wander by night, possessing defiled and malicious minds, and engaging in vile food and conduct; with faces like distorted moons, dark in complexion, extremely short, and clad in soiled garments stained with blood. (JPanc_1.33)
Thus ends the first arrow, titled "The Exposition of Castes and Other Categories," in the *Pañcasāyaka* composed by the crest-jewel of poets, Śrī Jyotirīśvara Kavi.
Now begins the second arrow:
"The Varieties of Sexual Union."

Men are to be known by their lengths and circumferences, and women by their characteristic marks and excellent limbs; and all [beings] are to be identified on every side by their proportions in finger-breadths (aṅgula) as described in the *Rasagṛha* and *Āruṇa*.

Furthermore, those of the rabbit, bull, and horse types are remembered by the wise, while those of the doe and the female elephant types are likewise distinguished; however, for fear of prolixity, these are now extracted here in brief.
The sexual union of a female rabbit and a female deer, or likewise that of a mare and a stallion, or a female elephant and a lordly bull-elephant, would be of a single uniform nature.
In this world, there is intense pleasure arising from mutual union; how then can a woman accept the practice of following her husband in death (anumaraṇa)? // JPanc_2.2 //
They say that a deer-male with a bull-female, or a bull-male with a mare-female—this pair is exceedingly high;
whereas a horse-male with a doe-female, or a cow-female with a boar-male—this lowly pair brings no satisfaction to the young couple.

They say that deer, horses, female elephants, and rabbits experience sexual pleasure in high and low degrees; yet, despite these differences in physical capacity, women do not fail to find satisfaction in it.
The aforementioned types of sexual union are classified as superior, middling, and inferior.
Equal passion between the woman and the man is praised; they consider two middling types to be mediocre.
Sexual union that is excessively high-pitched or excessively low-pitched is declared by those who know the art of love to be censurable.
In a sexual encounter known as *samākhyā*, pleasure should be equal; for a woman alone is satisfied even with two low-caste partners.
But neither men nor beautiful women find satisfaction in one who is either excessively high-born or excessively low-born.
Due to the difference in tempo, there are differences in sexual union (*surata*):
there is the intense tempo (*pracaṇḍavega*), then the moderate tempo (*madhyavega*), and another called the light tempo (*laghu*).
O lords of poets, they say that in this world, sexual union for both the man and the young woman is threefold.
Now the true nature of rabbits and other such animals is described:
Long-eyed, with stout bodies, small and even teeth, long ears, and eloquent speech; bearing a dark hue on their necks, knees, and the palms of their lotus-like hands;
eating little, requiring little purification, sleeping during the day, radiant, strong, playful, humble, quick in sexual union, and possessing merit—such are the rabbits.
With beautiful hair, gentle speech, fine attire, a very long neck, restless eyes,
hands that are deeply red, and even rows of teeth— this person endowed with such good fortune is described as a "deer."
With expansive forms, full of pride, and utterly addicted to the delights of sexual union; with beautiful limbs, broad chests, handsome features, and well-proportioned bellies;

fleshy, with restless eyes, extremely bold speech, and a steady, not too light, gait; irascible and possessing moderate speed—such bulls carry the phallus with their slightly elongated penises measured by fingers.
Bold in action, powerful, with white and even teeth, full faces, and large eyes; with long necks, arms, and thighs; devoted to the welfare of others, virtuous, and gentle in speech;

shameless yet of charming character, with a very wide gait and a passion for intense enjoyment—such horses, bearing the mark of eleven fingers as esteemed by young women, possess the qualities of the sattva nature. (JPanc_2.11)
The Description of the Nature of Deer-Women and Others:

She with soft limbs and long eyes, tender as a choice lotus-stalk, with long arms; she who bears a pair of hands as beautiful as red lotuses, with short waist and lovely hair; she with shapely hips, a neck like a conch-shell, and a broad pair of breasts—Jyotīśvara declares her here to be a *hariṇī* (deer-woman), for she possesses six fingers which indicate the abode of the God of Love. *JPanc_2.12*

With her head raised high due to her stooping gait, with a profusion of thick, tawny hair, and with eyes like shimmering blue lotuses; with a most lovely face, the weight of her lofty breasts, a navel deep as a whirlpool, and limbs languid from the burden of her hips—this very mare indeed bears the opening of the pleasure-cave, its fingers being the apertures.

With thick limbs, thick cheeks, very small eyes, and coarse, dark, sparse hair; with lips like the bimba fruit, stout arms, and hard, heavy breasts; with short finger-joints, she is exceedingly wicked, shameless, fond of donkey's flesh, and always has a restless face—this elephant-like woman (*hastinī*) is declared to be difficult to satisfy, and her secret parts measure twelve fingers in breadth. (JPanc 2.14)
Now, the specific stages of women's lives are described:
the wise call a girl "a child" until she is sixteen years of age;
from twenty, she is "young"; from thirty, "mature"; and from fifty, "old."

In dense darkness, a young girl brings delight during a first union; in the light, a young woman spreads pleasure during the act of amorous play. Even in the light, a mature woman brings joy with impetuosity, while in the dark, an old woman takes one's life and does not grant even the slightest comfort anywhere.
Now, the nature of women from specific regions is described:
A woman from a region near the mountains or the ocean is generally one whose limbs are coarse, who possesses many complexions, whose mind is fickle, who is fond of song, and who is flirtatious.
Furthermore, she should be enjoyed during the rainy season and the month of flowers, when she is gratified with heavy food, fragrant garlands, fine garments, and unguents for the body.
For throughout the entire body, even at night, she possesses a hidden knot of heat; her supreme hands are as red as the blooming lotus, and she is the beloved of the Lord of the Cool Abode (Śiva).
Saurāṣṭrī and the young woman of Kaliṅga may indeed be bilious, yet they should be enjoyed by men during the winter and the cool season without ceasing, according to their desire.

One should know her to be one whose sweet voice is like the soft warbling of a cuckoo, who is full-bodied, cool, and drowsy; whose body is as tender as a *śirīṣa* flower, whose face is glossy, and who is phlegmatic (*śleṣmalā*).
She is a young woman of Bengal, beautiful and lovely in form, apprehensive of cold and other such things; she possesses intense passion in autumn and is honored by men in the summer.

A woman from the Middle Country possesses pure conduct and diverse pleasures; she is a friend of varied enjoyment, detached from nails and teeth, yet devoted to the training in the arts. With a steady mind, she is her own kinswoman and an ocean of all that desire holds as its essence; such a passionate woman is of radiant appearance.
Skilled in the arrangement of embraces such as the *karakūcaka* and *karaja*, expert in all erotic postures and possessing the cleverness of wisdom,

moving with a speed that is neither too slow nor too heavy, and generally impassioned by desire— such a beautiful woman delights him even when she enjoys little, provided he does not consume [her] excessively.

With her divisions of soft speech, her tender limbs, and her freedom from fear during lovemaking, she possesses a gentle song of passion; the beloved, skilled in various modes of enjoyment, melts instantly— she is indeed said to be the Kaulī, celebrated as Vaṅgī and Gauḍī.

Delighted by the clapping of palms, thrilled by external enjoyment, accomplished through long dalliance, and won over by the words of a rogue; possessing the force of pleasure, manifesting the passion of love, and being fickle and slanderous—such would be this young woman of Cola.
With the complexion of a blue lotus petal, wearing beautiful earrings, with eyes like those of a startled doe and a face like a full-blown lotus;
she is fond of brief amorous dalliance, devoted to effortless enjoyment, possessing a most graceful gait, and dressed in lovely attire—this is the woman of Gujarat.
With eyes rolling languidly, her slender body possessing a divine form, she is difficult to satisfy in sexual union due to the intensity of her passion;
she becomes angry with her lover at the conclusion of lovemaking, and being fickle toward various men, she is a Sindhu woman of wicked character.

Causing horripilation with her touch, speaking wicked words, and being a vessel for perverse amorous play, she is surely the Night of Doom; such is the woman of Kośala and Avantī—a Purandhrī who, when distressed by passion, devours [her lover], as is heard in ancient tradition.

With voices as soft as cuckoos, delicate limbs, and great beauty, they are free from fear and shame; bold and independent, they are easily won over by light caresses—these lovely-limbed young women born in Cīna, Sauvīra, Bheda, Draviḍa, and Malaya. (JPanc_2.27)

Skilled in all amorous arts, possessing the power of success, good fortune, and subjugation, delighting in the pleasure of biting, clothing, and drinking, modest, expert at scratching with fingernails, charming with their fierce passion, and fragrant as flowers— such are the women of Madra and Talaṅga.

The women of Kāmarūpa and Aṅga are full of love for the pressure of passionate union; they are fierce, devoid of conventional signals such as scratching with nails, biting, pulling the hair, or embracing; their minds are naturally foul, and they find satisfaction in the mere touch of the palm of the hand. (JPanc 2.29)
Embracing her lover’s body firmly by the neck, she scratches it all over with her fingernails; pulling him by the hair, she kisses his lower lip incessantly and delivers blows with her fists.

She finds no satisfaction and does not quickly reach climax during sexual union; such a woman of fierce passion and boldness, whose pleasure is known through the arts of love, should be recognized as a Lāṭa or Karṇāṭa lady by the lords of scholars.

Mleccha women are wicked, their bodies foul-smelling, their sexual desire equal to that of beasts, devoid of kissing and embracing, and full of jealousy; so too are the women of the mountains, who are light-minded and devoted to trivial pleasure.

The women of Kashmir and Abhira are fragrant and highly skilled in all arts and flavors; therefore, women here must always be won over by those of sharp intellect in accordance with the customs of their respective regions. (JPanc 2.31)

He who thoroughly understands the entire essence of womanhood—the awakening of all the digits of the moon, the disposition of her nature, the subjugation of deer and other creatures, and the complete wonder of the arts of amorous passion—and who thus correctly perceives the conduct of loving women according to their regional customs for as long as he lives, becomes the lord of her life within her heart for her happiness. (JPanc 2.32)
An Examination of the Varieties of the Vagina:

By touch, the vagina of young women may be like a lotus; within it, there may be a region shaped like a pill. Furthermore, the vagina may be covered with folds of skin, and its internal region may be as rough as a cow's tongue. (JPanc 2.33)
The first [type] has been declared by the lords of poets to be most excellent; the middle one is indeed taught as being of middling quality;
but the remaining two are always said to be censurable by those who know the essence of the arts of amorous play during the festivals of sexual union.
Fire never attains peace through wood; the ocean does not cease with abundant waters;
nor does Death find satisfaction with living beings in this world; indeed, even a woman is never satiated by men.

Therefore, a man skilled in the arts of love, having mastered all illusions achievable by his own body, should focus solely on captivating their minds; for indeed, no one truly knows the heart of women.
An Examination of the Varieties of Joy:

The joy that is always augmented by various objects such as garlands, sandalwood, fine garments, and delightful foods and drinks, is known by the foremost of poets as "joy born of sense-objects"; it is always described as being made beautiful through its association with similarity. (JPanc 2.37)

That [skill] which is cultivated by slender-waisted women in the practice of hunting, the arts, the worship of the gods, play, dance, song, and service—by virtue of the proficiency gained through repeated practice—is called *ābhyāsikī* by the ancient poets. (JPanc 2.38)
Women are the causes for the destruction of passion in men;

yet, due to poverty, suffering, fear, distress, loss of honor, disease, agitation, anger, emaciation, and so forth, even powerful lords abandon passion here in this world. For fear of prolixity, the entire transformation of this matter has not been recounted.
Thus ends the second arrow in the *Pañcasāyaka* composed by the illustrious poet Jyotīśvara, the crest-jewel of poets.
Now begins the third arrow: Formulas for removing bodily odors.
First, a man should apply body-unguents to his limbs, as should a woman, for the sake of the pleasure of sexual union;
therefore, I shall first describe the entire procedure for perfumes for the sake of the graceful lover.
Harītakī, lodhra, leaves of mariṣṭa, saptacchada, and the pulp of the pomegranate—
this is declared by the lords of poets to be an ointment for a woman that removes the foul odor of the body.
An ointment made from equal parts of *harītakī*, sandalwood, *mustā*, *nāgara*, *uśīra*, *lodhra*,
and *amaya-rātri* quickly destroys the sweat and body odor of both men and women.

This formulation—consisting of *harītakī*, *śrīphala*, *musta*, *bimbī* fruits, and the seeds of *pūtaka-rañjana*—swiftly and forcibly destroys even the most excessive foul odor of the armpits and other areas. (JPanc 3.4)
Having smeared her body with sandalwood, uśīra, bilva leaves, kola, akṣa, marrow, aguru, and nāgapuṣpa flowers, a woman quickly destroys even long-established odor. (JPanc 3.5)
"By anointing their bodies with the powdered mixture of saffron, uśīra, śirīṣa, and aloeswood,
men in the summer will perhaps never experience the flow of sweat," so said King Bhoja.
This is the oil of great fragrance (*mahāparimala*).

First, one should place *bilva* leaves, then *maruvaka* flowers, and then *aśoka* flowers into a jar of sesame oil, adding them continuously and facing the sun. One should repeatedly and with care add *ketakī* flowers at the end; in this way, men should prepare this oil of great fragrance for the sake of success.
The description of fragrant substances for bathing:
By anointing oneself with a paste composed of gold-leaf (*svarṇa*), ambuda, uśīra, miśī, and pathyā,
a man who has bathed attains fragrance itself, and after one month, his hair becomes singularly pure.
For the increase of fragrance and luster, a person should bathe after applying a paste made of *pathyā*, *rasālāmalakī* fruits, *jambū* and *jīmūtadala* leaves, along with *māṃsī*.
These are the formulations that produce fragrance for the body:
one part each of *harītakī* and water, a fourth part of *vanecara*, and half of that part of *nakha*; this is the "Madana-prakāśa" fragrance. (JPanc 3.10)
Cardamom, śaṭī, cinnamon leaves, sandalwood, water-lily, abhayā, moon-plant, and nutmeg—
this highly fragrant mixture, fit for the king of the gods, is renowned as a perfume for the purpose of enchanting men.
Having ground together the fat of a black antelope, saffron, thick water, iron, turmeric, and ushira root in equal parts,
this beloved ointment was proclaimed by the most excellent of ancient masters of poetry as pleasing to gods and men alike.
Having ground together uśīra, kṛṣṇāguru, and sandalwood in equal parts with water infused with patra leaves,
these spread upon the bodies of graceful women a fragrance equal to that of śrīkhaṇḍa.
The most excellent applications of fragrant substances:
jasmine, karkaṭa, red sandalwood, solid *śrīvāsa*, and *śaileyaka*, combined with musk, *kanaka*, *amataṅgakusuma*, and *sthauṇeyaka*— these,

when mixed with moon-bright [camphor] and ground with the juice of *parṇaja*, should always be prepared as an auspicious body-unguent by those skilled in the entire range of perfumery for the use of a lord of the earth.

Four parts of *pathyā* (harītakī), one part of *jalamuca* (musta), four parts of *vyādhi* (viḍaṅga), two parts of *śaśin* (karpūra) with *sthauṇeya*, five parts of *śilodbhava* (manahśilā), and one part of *nakha*—this is declared by those who know the science of fragrance as the preparation known as *kastūrīdala*. (JPanc 3.15)
Four parts of *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan), one part of *jalamuca* (musta grass), and three parts each of *śrīkhaṇḍa* (white sandalwood), *aguru* (aquilaria), *jātī* (nutmeg), and *mṛgamada* (musk)—

all these well-ground together with equal portions of *māṃsī* (spikenard), *padma* (lotus), *tuṣāra* (camphor), and *vālaka* (vetiver)— are here declared to be the excellent preparation known as Saurabhyagarbha.
Formulas for mouth-perfumes:
The essence of the heart of *rasālā* and *jambū* fruit, together with *karkaṭa* and honey, when held within the mouth of a person at night, produces the pleasant fragrance of the mouth. (JPanc 3.17)
A small pill should be prepared from jaggery, cinnamon, cardamom, nakha, nutmeg, and cloves, combined with gold;

When a maiden is invited and honored with worship, clothed in excellent garments by the father himself, and given with respect according to the prescribed rite to a worthy suitor who is endowed with learning, character, discernment, noble lineage, humility, and proper conduct, that is declared by the preeminent sages to be the "Brāhma" marriage, the most excellent among the others.
